nameStory: The 'Neat Aeolid' gets its common name from its tidy, organized appearance - unlike many sea slugs that look wild and chaotic, this species has a remarkably orderly arrangement of its body parts. The scientific name 'concinna' actually means 'neat' or 'elegant' in Latin, so both the common and scientific names celebrate this little creature's well-groomed look!
description: The Neat Aeolid is a tiny sea slug that looks like a living jewel crawling along the ocean floor. These marine creatures are nudibranchs, which means 'naked gills' - they breathe through colorful, finger-like projections on their backs instead of having hidden gills like fish. They're soft-bodied mollusks related to snails, but they've lost their shells through evolution. Most are quite small, typically less than an inch long.

idTips.label: Finger-like projections
idTips.description: Look for rows of slender, finger-like structures called cerata covering the back - these feel soft and squishy if gently touched and often have colorful tips

idTips.label: Smooth, translucent body
idTips.description: The main body appears smooth and somewhat see-through, with a jelly-like texture that's firm but yielding to gentle pressure

idTips.label: Two pairs of tentacles
idTips.description: Notice four horn-like projections on the head - two smooth oral tentacles near the mouth and two rhinophores that often look wrinkled or folded

idTips.label: Crawling movement
idTips.description: Moves with a smooth gliding motion across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail but feeling slightly sticky if you let it crawl on your finger

idTips.label: Orderly arrangement
idTips.description: The cerata are arranged in neat, organized clusters rather than scattered randomly - this gives it a tidy, well-groomed appearance

habitat: Look for Neat Aeolids in shallow coastal waters of New England, particularly in tide pools, on rocky shores, and among seaweed beds. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found crawling on hydroids (tiny colonial animals) which they feed on. You're most likely to spot them during low tide when tide pools are exposed.

seasonality.spring: Active in tide pools as water temperatures begin to warm. Look for them on hydroids and among early-season seaweed growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and abundant. Best time for tide pool exploration when they're actively feeding and moving.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be found deeper in tide pools or under rocks as temperatures begin to cool. Colors may appear more vibrant.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible and active. Most individuals move to deeper water or hide in protected crevices, making them difficult to observe.

funFact: Neat Aeolids are solar-powered animals! Many species can steal chloroplasts (the green, energy-making parts) from the algae they eat and store them in those finger-like projections on their backs, essentially turning themselves into part-plant, part-animal hybrids that can photosynthesize their own food.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small nudibranchs, but remember the 'neat' part of their name - their cerata are arranged in tidy rows rather than scattered chaotically. Unlike true sea anemones, they move around actively rather than staying anchored in one spot.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Greek, referring to their exposed breathing structures. Don't worry if you see various spellings of technical terms - marine biology naming can be complex, and these creatures are often reclassified as scientists learn more about their relationships.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cuthonella species documented in New England, compare it with other aeolid nudibranchs in the region. The Neat Aeolid's distinguishing feature is its particularly orderly arrangement of cerata and overall tidy appearance. Other aeolids may have similar finger-like projections but lack the neat, organized clustering that gives this species its name.
